---
title: "Comparing Penalty Functions"
toc: true
---

## Description

The SIMP penalty maps the design density `x` to the effective stiffness
material used in the finite-element assembly. A steeper penalty suppresses
intermediate ("gray") densities, but too steep a penalty makes the problem
non-convex and hard to optimize. TopOpt.jl provides four penalties:

- `PowerPenaltyFun(p)` — the classic SIMP power law `x^p`.
- `RationalPenaltyFun(p)` — `x / (1 + p(1 - x))`, smoother than the power law
  for the same exponent.
- `SinhPenaltyFun(p)` — `sinh(p·x) / sinh(p)`, another smooth alternative.
- `ProjectedPenaltyFun(penalty, proj)` — applies a projection (default
  `HeavisideProjectionFun(10)`) before the penalty, pushing toward a near-binary
  design.

This tutorial compares their curves, their effect on the optimized design, and
the sensitivity of the result to the penalty parameter.

## Setup

```{julia}
#| output: false
using TopOpt, LinearAlgebra
using WGLMakie
WGLMakie.activate!(; resize_to=:parent)
using Bonito
if haskey(ENV, "QUARTO_PROJECT_DIR")
    Bonito.Page(exportable=true, offline=true)
else
    Bonito.browser_display()
end
display_app(app) = display(app)
```

`WGLMakie.activate!(; resize_to=:parent)` selects the browser renderer and fills the Quarto output column. `Bonito.Page(exportable=true, offline=true)` embeds the assets needed by `visualize(...; static=true)` in the Quarto output, so the visualization does not require a running Julia process.

## The penalty curves

```{julia}
#| output: true
p = 3.0
penalties = [
    ("power", PowerPenaltyFun(p)),
    ("rational", RationalPenaltyFun(p)),
    ("sinh", SinhPenaltyFun(p)),
    ("projected", ProjectedPenaltyFun(PowerPenaltyFun(p))),
]
for x in (0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0)
    vals = [round(P(x), digits=3) for (_, P) in penalties]
    println("x=$x → ", join(["$(n)=$v" for ((n, _), v) in zip(penalties, vals)], "  "))
end
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-penalties-curves
#| fig-cap: "Penalty functions (p = 3): stiffness multiplier P(x) vs design density x"
using Makie
xs = range(0.0, 1.0; length=101)
fig = Figure()
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel="design density x", ylabel="penalty P(x)")
for (name, P) in penalties
    lines!(ax, xs, P.(xs); label=name)
end
axislegend(ax)
display_app(fig)
```

At `x = 0.5` the rational and sinh penalties are milder than the power law
(more intermediate stiffness), while the projected penalty is already nearly
binary.

## Optimize with each penalty

We solve the same Half MBB compliance problem with each penalty (exponent 3)
and measure the resulting grayness — the fraction of elements in the
intermediate band `(0.1, 0.9)`.

```{julia}
#| output: false
E, ν, f = 1.0, 0.3, 1.0
nels = (60, 20)
N = prod(nels)
V = 0.5
rmin = 2.0

problem = HalfMBB(nels, (1.0, 1.0), E, ν, f)
grayness(x) = count(0.1 .< x .< 0.9) / length(x)

function solve_with(penalty)
    solver = FEASolver(DirectSolver, problem; xmin=0.001, penalty=penalty)
    filter = DensityFilterFun(solver; rmin=rmin)
    comp = ComplianceFun(solver)
    volfrac = VolumeFun(solver)
    obj = x -> comp(filter(PseudoDensities(x)))
    constr = x -> volfrac(filter(PseudoDensities(x))) - V
    model = Model(obj)
    addvar!(model, zeros(N), ones(N))
    add_ineq_constraint!(model, constr)
    r = optimize(model, MMA87(), fill(V, N);
        options=MMAOptions(; maxiter=120, tol=Tolerance(; kkt=1e-4, f=1e-4)))
    topo = filter(PseudoDensities(r.minimizer)).x
    return obj(r.minimizer), constr(r.minimizer) + V, grayness(topo), topo
end
```

```{julia}
#| output: true
results = Dict{String,Any}()
for (name, P) in penalties
    c, vol, g, topo = solve_with(P)
    results[name] = topo
    println("$(lpad(name, 10)): compliance = $(round(c, digits=2)), vol = $(round(vol, digits=3)), gray = $(round(g, digits=3))")
end
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-penalties-power
#| fig-cap: "PowerPenaltyFun(p=3): standard SIMP result"
fig_p = visualize(problem; static=true, topology=results["power"])
display_app(fig_p)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-penalties-projected
#| fig-cap: "ProjectedPenaltyFun: near-binary design"
fig_proj = visualize(problem; static=true, topology=results["projected"])
display_app(fig_proj)
```

The power, rational, and sinh penalties produce comparable topologies with
varying amounts of gray; the projected penalty produces a noticeably crisper
design.

## Parameter sensitivity

Ramping the exponent of the power-law penalty trades stiffness for binary
crispness. We sweep `p` and report the grayness and final compliance.

```{julia}
#| output: true
for p in (2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 5.0)
    c, vol, g, _ = solve_with(PowerPenaltyFun(p))
    println("p=$p: compliance = $(round(c, digits=2)), gray = $(round(g, digits=3))")
end
```

## Guidance

- **Power law** is the default and the most widely reported; `p = 3` is the
  standard choice for 2D continuum problems.
- **Rational / sinh** penalties transition more smoothly, which can help
  continuation strategies converge from a uniform start.
- **Projected penalty** is the go-to when a crisp 0/1 design matters more than
  a slight stiffness penalty; combine it with a continuation on the projection
  `β` (see the `projected_filter` tutorial) for best results.
